newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel halts peace talks after suicide bombs.
newsitem.headline: Israel halts peace talks after suicide bombs.

text.p: Fifteen people were blown apart in a packed Jewish market in Jerusalem on Wednesday in a twin suicide bombing that prompted Israel to halt peace talks with President Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority.

Police said the two Moslem militant bombers, who were among the dead, strolled into the Mahane Yehuda market dressed in jackets and ties with 10-kilo (22-pound) bombs hidden in attache cases. Around 170 people were wounded, police added.
The death toll was the highest in an attack in Israel since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu won election last year on a pledge to bolster security.
His spokesman, Shai Bazak, told Israel Radio after a crisis session of the security cabinet there could be no peace talks as long as Arafat failed to pursue the "fight against terrorism".
"At this stage no steps will be taken (in the peace process) so long as the Palestinian Authority doesn't take steps it committed to," Bazak said.
Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah in reaction told Reuters the authority had been combatting militants.
"We ask the Israeli government to implement the agreements signed under the auspices of President Clinton because this is the only way to save the peace process," he added.

A leaflet issued in the name of the Moslem militant Hamas movement claimed the attack and demanded that Israel free all Palestinian prisoners by Sunday night including Hamas founder Sheik Ahmed Yassin.
Bazak made clear that Israel held Arafat's administration responsible for failing to crack down on Hamas and other militant groups in Palestinian self-rule areas.

"The ministerial committee on national security sees the Palestinian Authority as responsible for acts of terrorism and for the murder of innocent civilians in Jerusalem in that it didn't take the steps that it was obligated to take, among them the war against terrorist organisations and their infrastructure," Bazak said.

Israel and the Palestinians agreed earlier this week to resume talks on carrying out interim peace accords already signed on such issues as a Gaza airport and seaport and safe passage for Palestinians between the West Bank and Gaza.

That move prompted renewed optimism abroad that negotiations stalled for four months might be back on course and an announcement in Washington that President Bill Clinton was sending his envoy Dennis Ross back to the region.

The White House said it was postponing the trip, planned for Thursday, to allow Israel to mourn its dead as both Clinton and Netanyahu piled pressure on Arafat to crack down on Hamas and other anti-Israeli Moslem militant groups.

"The only answer can and must be concrete steps by the Palestinian Authority to increase security operations and the strengthening of security cooperation between Palestinians and Israelis," Clinton told a White House news conference.

Arafat condemned the killings as an attack "against the peace process, against the Palestinians, and against the Israelis". He told Reuters he was urging Netanyahu not to give up on the search for peace.
"We will do our best to face these terrorist activities as we have done in the past and will do in the future," he said.
A senior Palestinian security official said arrests of militants had already begun.
Netanyahu earlier rejected Arafat's telephoned condolences, telling the Palestinian leader that sorrow would not suffice.
"We aren't ready to accept that murderous acts will be part of our daily lives every few weeks and months and we will await suitable steps," he said after visiting wounded in hospital.

The near-simultaneous explosions, about 40 metres (yards) apart, brought the worst death toll in the Jewish state since a spate of Moslem militant suicide bombings in February and March 1996 killed 59 people.
The Israeli army said it had responded by sealing off the West Bank and Gaza Strip and barring Palestinians from leaving their home locations.
The last big bombing to rock Israel, on March 21, killed three Israeli women along with the Palestinian Hamas bomber, and wounded 42 people at an outdoor cafe in Tel Aviv.
That attack happened three days after Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement on a hilltop in Arab East Jerusalem known to Israelis as Har Homa and to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Israeli-Palestinian peace talks have been in crisis since then, with Arafat insisting negotiations on a final peace agreement cannot take place until settlement activity stops.
Israel has countered that the Palestinian Authority must control militants. It now accuses it of actively promoting violence.
The Hamas claim said the bombings had been carried out by the "Izz el-Deen al-Qassam Brigades martyrs unit for emancipation of prisoners".

Hamas sources said the suicide bombers came from the West Bank and staged the attack to avenge a Jewish woman's pasting of posters depicting the Moslem Prophet Mohammed as a pig on storefronts in the West Bank town of Hebron last month.

They said it also was in retaliation for the publication in an Israeli science magazine of a photomontage of the Virgin Mary with a cow's head. The photo, to illustrate a story on cloning, angered Palestinian Christians.
